title: Gravitational Force and Elastic Spring Force
seo_title: Primary 6 Science: Gravity and Spring Force Worksheets (PSLE Practice with Answers)
standard_code: Primary 6: Interaction of forces (Gravitational force and elastic spring force)
standard_text: Recognise that gravitational force is the pull of the Earth on objects and that the weight of an object is the gravitational force acting on it. Investigate the effect of a force on a spring: the extension of a spring increases as the load increases (summary of the MOE Primary Science Syllabus).
meta_desc: Free Primary 6 science worksheets for Singapore pupils on gravitational force, weight in newtons, spring balances and the extension of springs. PSLE practice with answers.
key_big: Gravity pulls; springs push or pull back.
key_sub: Weight is in newtons; extension grows with the load.
body_html:
How to think about it

Gravitational force is the pull of the Earth on objects. Weight is the gravitational force on an object.

  • Weight is measured in newtons (N) with a spring balance. On Earth, 1 kg weighs about 10 N.
  • A stretched or compressed spring exerts an elastic spring force back towards its original length.
  • Extension = stretched length − original length. A bigger load gives a bigger extension, until the spring is overstretched.
Example

A spring is 12 cm long. With a 3 N load it is 18 cm. What is the extension?

18 − 12

Answer: 6 cm.

Example

A 2 kg bag of rice: what is its weight on Earth?

About 10 N for every kg

2 × 10

Answer: About 20 N.

Common mistakes

  • Measuring weight in kilograms. Weight is a force, measured in newtons.
  • Giving the total length instead of the extension.
  • Thinking heavier objects fall much faster. Without air resistance, they fall at the same rate.
  • Thinking gravity only acts on falling objects. It acts on everything all the time.

faq.q: What is the difference between mass and weight?
faq.a: Mass is the amount of matter in an object, in kilograms. Weight is the pull of gravity on it, a force in newtons.

faq.q: How do I find the extension of a spring?
faq.a: Subtract the original length from the stretched length. For example, 16 cm − 10 cm = 6 cm.

faq.q: What happens if a spring is overstretched?
faq.a: It may not go back to its original length, and it no longer stretches evenly with the load.
